doc.title: Frank Wess interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 29, 1995

title: The blues and advice to young musicians
summary: Wess says the blues come from environmental sounds, singers and guitarists, and that students must study technique.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: What would you say to our young musicians about the blues?
What do you mean about the blues?
Try and make them turn green. That’s the best thing I can tell you.
As a form of music, was it, when were you aware of learning—is it something that you played on early in your career as an improviser?

Yeah, well you know, I came up in the southwest. It’s something you come up with just like anything else, like water. You can understand. And there was a lot of that influence came from blues singers and guitar players and sounds. Like all from things in Africa, it comes from field sounds and in this country a lot of things used to come from train sounds, train whistles. And as you know, you could always tell who the engineer was by the way he blew the whistle. So a lot of that comes from sounds that you hear in the environment. They all come. And guitar players imitate blues singers, and it all gets incorporated in the music. It’s a way of life. And that’s what it is. The only thing that I would say to all students I mean is that you have to study and be efficient technically, and you know you have to have endurance and there is so much that you have to do for so long. But really, a lot of that isn’t music, you know?
